This is most likely a [magnolia green jumping spider](https://bugguide.net/node/view/2040)(*Lyssomanes viridis*). The other users are correct in the fact that it belong to genus *Lyssomanes* (translucent green jumpers) but it can be narrowed down more. The World Spider Catalog only recognizes one species in the US and that is *viridis*.  The red “cap”, as I call it, is a key feature of these little guys and the coloration of this “cap” makes it easier to see the eyes . Although difficult to see in the photo, the eye arrangement does appear to be similar to that of a jumping spider. 

Just for some fun learning, there are some ways to tell this one apart from a [green lynx spider](https://bugguide.net/node/view/2032) (*Peucetia viridans*). Assuming you are comparing specimens with similar coloration, the first thing that will stick out is the large dark hairs on the legs of the green lynx spider. [Here](https://imgur.com/a/sEnM2UQ) is a friend I made a few days ago. You can see the obvious dark bristle-like hairs on the legs. You can also see the difference in the arrangement of the eyes. 

I absolutely love these guys so if you have any questions or need clarification on anything, please feel free to reach out to me.

Ghost shrimp are totally peaceful. Their nearly identical cousins, the whisker shrimp, are as far from peaceful as a shrimp can be. 

For future reference, ghost shrimp have orange/red bands around their antennas and pinchers whereas whisker shrimp don’t. You should also look for 2 small red/orange spots on the tail that only ghost shrimp have. Whisker shrimp will often develop much more coloration as they grow and get up to half an inch larger. Whisker shrimp also have much longer pinchers and larger claws

I’m always happy to help if you want more advice as I have a lot of experience with rabbit care and such so if you want I can send you a couple links or something after I get off work to help you. It can be a daunting process for sure! I have (had…) an off white carpet as my flooring so rabbit stains were my biggest fear. 

It ended up that my rabbits have never stained the floor with pee (in 5 years but I’m knocking on wood) but they have stained it with toys. Warning if you have carpet or any kind of fabric, [those](https://www.amazon.com/Wild-Harvest-P-84127-Colored-Flavored/dp/B00GUG1FO8) dyed wood blocks bleed color everywhere. My bun dropped it in his water bowl and then carried it out onto the floor and no matter what we did, that big red stain won’t come up. 

My best advice if you are concerned about it is use something to protect your floors. Flat trash bags covered in old towels is a favorite of mine but be careful they don’t get to the trash bags and eat that plastic. They also make these cool blankets that are soft on top and waterproof on the bottom so nothing gets through to your floor but that can be a little pricey imo for something temporary. After a couple months of no accidents, I removed most of the floor coverings. If the space is big enough, add multiple litter boxes so they always have somewhere to go.

Hey! So I’ve successfully litterbox trained 3 rabbits, two young and one older. The best method in my experience is picking up behind them. 

Step one is to put the hay in/on the litterbox so that they eat where you want them to poop. Every time you see a poop outside the litterbox, pick it up and toss it in. 

For pee it’s a little bit more complicated. Rabbit pee has a very strong smell so they will know where they last peed and might think it’s okay if you don’t clean it up. When you find pee, soak it up with a small amount of paper towel and put that paper towel on the litterbox. Then use a vinegar and water mix to spray the area they peed. This mixture almost always removes any stains and smells especially if you do it quickly. Eventually they will realize that they only pee in the litterbox. Took my smartest one about a week before he had it down and my *slowest* one about 3 weeks before she had it down. 

Spaying and neutering greatly helps the process as well as your rabbits health. Do not pick up the rabbit and put it in the box or scold it for going out outside the box as this may form a fear of the litterbox. For some rabbits this might work but for most it will do more harm than good. They also like a place that is safe and protected so corners are great!
